South African Opera Singers and the Belvedere Competition June 2016 [4746]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Belvedere Competition

What launched Pretty Yende into the world operatic spotlight, of course she has the voice and the talent , but it was through the exposure she gained when singing in the Belvedere Competition.

The International Hans Gabor Belvedere Singing Competition is THE “springboard” for a career in opera: Past participants and prize winners include Angela Gheorghiu, Ildikó Raimondi, Elina Garanča, Lado Ataneli and Peter Edelmann. Recent winners include Italian tenor Antonio Poli, who made his debut in 2011 at the Salzburg Festival alongside Anna Netrebko and Piotr Beczala. Soprano Rachel Willis-Sørensen, the 1st prize winner of the International Hans Gabor Belvedere Singing Competition in 2011, made her highly-acclaimed Royal Opera House Covent Garden debut in 2012. And Pretty Yende, winner of all main prizes in 2009, makes an international career with engagements at the most renowned opera houses in the world.

In 2015 the qualifying rounds are held in 63 cities world-wide. The finals take place in cooperation with the Dutch National Opera & Ballet, on 4 July 2015. The singers continue to be judged by a jury consisting of artistic and casting directors from the world's most prestigious opera houses including the Royal Opera House Covent Garden in London, Gran Teatre del Liceu Barcelona, Deutsche Oper Berlin, Osterfestspiele Salzburg, Metropolitan Opera New York, to name a few.

Tenor Levy Strauss Sekgopane, a graduate from the Cape Town Opera School,won the Belvedere singing competition this year, in which three of the new wave of South African singers were finalists, the Montserrat Caballé competition in Spain, and the Southern African Music Rights Organisation’s Best Western Art Music singer prize.

Next year the Belvedere competition will be hosted in Cape Town, the first time in Africa.

This is a great coup for the country.

My proposal is to do an insert following South African competitors in this competition and looking at why our small country, where the arts are underfunded and unrecognized are making such an impact on the world wide opera scene.

I have been in touch with the organisers and they are very happy to grant us permission. Of course we hope that a South African will win the competition but we can't bank on this. Pretty Yende is coming to SA in March for a concert with Sunnyboyoy Dlala, another South African singer who has made it to the big time overseas. I have contacted Cape Town Opera to see whether we can interview her in March to use in the programme of the Belvedere Competition.

Press Release:


Opera’s Own Olympics
The Belvedere International Singing Competition, recently held in Cape Town, is considered the ‘Olympics of Opera’. The event attracted more than 1 000 young singers from 70 countries. Carte Blanche catches up with previous winner and world opera star Pretty Yende, and meets local talent hitting all the right notes from Milan to the Met!


Script:


Belvedere Script

V/O 8secs
The venue was Amsterdam, the year, 2015.
The occasion - the annual Hans Gabor Belvedere Singing Competition.
13 secs
Among the contestants - a young graduate of the Cape Town Opera School, Free State born Levy Strauss Sekgapane. How would his undiscovered voice compare with a thousand others from across the world?

Levy
“I thought I had no chance, when I arrived there the first time, beautiful people, beautiful sopranos, tenors and bases they walk with they are so proud and of course you are intimidated by them.

V/O 14 secs
He needn’t have been intimidated. Levy Sekgapane won the prestigious competition. Yet another South African operatic sensation – one of those incredible voices coming from nowhere – without resources, or childhood training.

Levy
“I was just speechless, I just cried actually because it was the beginning of my life, it was the beginning of a new life.”

V/O 7 secs
From Amsterdam it was Berlin, Dresden, Rome. Levy stood at the brink of an international operatic career.


Link
The Belvedere Competition is arguably the most prestigious in the world 854 singers applied and the preliminary rounds were held in 70 cities across the globe. This year Cape Town is playing host to the finals, the first time they have been held outside Europe.

V/O 18 seconds
Founded by the legendary Austrian conductor Hans Gabor in 1982. The contest is the springboard for a career in opera. Here managers and agents from around the world scout for new talent.

Hans Gabor’s widow, Isabella, continues his legacy, showcasing inchoate voices to the opera world.

Isabella
“It became a bit of a stock exchange for singers. I think it the stepping stone for young singers to help them in their career.”

V/O 19 secs
It’s more than that: winning the Belvedere competition almost guarantees operatic stardom. Tonight, these Cape Town opera graduates are hoping they’ll be catapulted into a new world.

Lukhanyo Moyake happened upon opera by accident – he heard a CD of the Three Tenors.

“And then I said I want to sing like that. In the choirs I always tried to be a soloist.”

V/O 12 secs
Noluvuyiso Mpofu has a background in choral singing. She first heard opera at an Eisteddfod at high school in Port Elizabeth.

Noluvuyiso
“I remember sitting there, listening to this girl singing and then she was singing opera the music was just beautiful and I just said there and then Ok I love this and this is what I want to do.”

V/O 3 secs
She decided she needed to embrace this art form.

“I went to the library, and then I researched opera everything about opera and then borrowed a dvd from someone and then I just learn the aria from the dvd and that was it for me.”

V/O 18 seconds
Self-taught, she came second in the Eisteddfod when she was 17 and after school set off to study opera in Cape Town.

The University of Cape Town’s Opera School is akin to New York’s Julliard Opera School and has nurtured many talented young stars who’ve made it abroad.

Link
There were fears some time ago that in this country that opera would die a Eurocentric death but South Africa has a strong choral tradition and that is why our singers continue hitting the high notes on the international stage.

Pretty
“The Belvedere competition for me opened all the doors that I can ever think of.”

V/O 8 secs
Pretty Yende won the Hans Gabor competition in 2009.
Her musical journey began in the unlikely town of Piet Retief in Mpumalanga.



Pretty
“When I started singing the whole family was excited but most of the family members like my uncle was so surprised to hear me singing opera and he said you are singing this music, this music is for rich people and at the time I had no idea that this kind of music only belonged to people of a certain class.

V/O 18 secs
Yende has conquered the Met in New York, Milan’s La Scala - where she was artist-in-residence for four years - and the Paris Opera. She has shared the stage with names like Bocelli and Domingo and she recently debuted I Puritani in Zurich to rave reviews.

“The South Africans are doing well because they all come from a huge choral tradition.”

V/O 12 secs
Singing, it seems, is a natural form of expression to many South Africans. But when told Levy his parents that he wanted to pursue a career in an art form they knew very little about they were naturally concerned.

Levy
“Every Parent wishes their child was a doctor or a teacher or something, something they could see in life, but if a child said, mama I want to be an actor, they will be like “what?” How are you going to do that, so they didn’t know what to expect really.





V/O 12 secs
With his stellar success his parents fears are allayed, like Pretty South African opera singers are highly sought after overseas.

Prof Kamal Khan is head of the Cape Town Opera School.

Professor Kamal
“This is one of the increasingly few countries where people sing operatically as a natural response to emotion, in a similar way to the way it was in Italy when these works were first being written. Like it isn’t necessarily in Italy today for example it’s a growth business here also because young men don’t regard being involved in the arts as not masculine they respect the achievement and respect the athleticism of it.

Helgor ( Belvedere Competition Manager)

“South Africans are emotional. Emotions are necessary for the arts and for opera especially. And if you are able to bring emotion to the audience that is the best gift that you can have.”

V/O 12 secs
Back at the Belvedere, Noluvuyiso is a bundle of nerves at the semi finals. Last year she got into the finals. This year she is up 50 other superb singers, capable of extreme vocal control.


Noluvuyiso
“I felt that I didn’t do as well but then when they said I sent through to the finals, I was oh Yay. I was so happy.”

V/O

Link
Despite being at the tip of the continent and 1000 of kms away from the opera capitals of the world, South Africa is well represented in the finals. Of the 16 competitors who made it through to the deciding rounds 4 are from this country.

V/O
More than any other single country represented at the competition.


Pretty
“The talent in South Africa is what separates us from the world, there is just something so special about the vocal quality that each and every South African young singer has that the world is not so used to.

V/O 6 secs
There’s good news for Noluvuyiso at this year’s Belvedere. She won the audience award and came second in the competition.

Noluvuyiso
“Everyone sang their hearts out and just to be given a position in the top 3 is amazing.”

V/O 5 secs
Last year’s winner, Levy Sekgapane, is now based in Germany and is living his dream.

Levy
“I feel like a king when I am on stage, I feel like I have the whole world under my hands.

Promos
Promo 1 - 10 secs
What makes South Africans naturally suited to opera? Pretty Yende started life in Piet Retief and is now hitting the high notes in Milan, New York and Zurich.

Promo 2 – 15 secs

“I feel like a king when I am on stage.”

Winning the Belvedere Singing Competition thrust Levy Sekgapane into the operatic spotlight. South African opera stars are charming the world, singing with the emotion of a country and its people.

Promo 3 – 15 secs

South African are hitting the high notes and the world is taking notice - the Belvedere Competition is arguably the most prestigious in the world . It was held in Cape Town recently where 89 international opera singers competed for this coveted award.

Promo 4 – 11 secs
Pretty Yende and Levy Sekgapane – from small towns to the big world of opera
